title: The Mediterranean Salt Crisis, When the Door Closed
description: Tonight is about a sea and its door. About six million years ago the Mediterranean was cut off, or nearly cut off, from the Atlantic, and the rocks under its floor keep what followed: gypsum around its edges, a layer of salt a kilometre or more thick in its deep basins, and then, a little over five million years ago, the return of the Atlantic. It begins at the Strait of Gibraltar as it is today, and it ends at the same strait.

It is told through places and rock: a drilling ship in the early nineteen seventies; a filament no longer than two millimetres, lying in a crystal of gypsum in Piedmont; a last stage that may have been a lake or a sea; a channel under the strait, two hundred kilometres long; a low white cliff in Sicily where one kind of rock stops and another begins; and caves in the Italian hills.

A good deal of tonight is honestly unsettled. How far the water fell, whether about fifteen hundred metres or about six hundred, whether the deep basins ever dried, how long the salt took to form, what closed and opened the door, whether the last stage was a lake or a sea, and how fast the sea came back are all argued over. The famous version, that the Mediterranean dried up and was quickly refilled, is only one picture, and the episode says so.

It stays gentle throughout. Nothing hunts, nothing is in peril, no one stands on a shore, and the refilling is told only through what the rock keeps: a groove, a field of smooth ridges, a line in a cliff.
You do not need to follow any of it closely. If you're asleep before the cliff in Sicily, that's the intended use.
